newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: Flat NZ jobs data surprises markets, steadies kiwi.
newsitem.headline: Flat NZ jobs data surprises markets, steadies kiwi.

text.p: Stronger than expected New Zealand jobs data is likely to help the beleaguered kiwi dollar stabilise around current levels, analysts said on Tuesday.

Monetary conditions, as measured by the New Zealand dollar and 90-day bank bill rates, tightened on Tuesday as markets were caught off guard by data showing flat June quarter employment rather than the downturn most observers had forecast.
Statistics New Zealand said seasonally adjusted employment grew by a narrow 0.2 percent in the June quarter, while economists' average forecast had been for a 0.15 percent fall.
The data showed an economy that remained in a trough but not trapped as deeply as some private sector observers had expected.

The headline unemployment rate for the quarter was 6.7 percent, up slightly from 6.5 percent in the previous three months and well above the year-ago rate of 6.0 percent. Economists had predicted a much sharper jump in unemployment, out to 6.9 percent.

They were even more surprised by a 2.5 percent rise in the number of hours worked. Most had judged a recent Reserve Bank of NZ (RBNZ) projection of a 1.9 percent rise as too high, and several forecast a rise in hours worked of under one percent.
By the close the kiwi dollar had established a steady level of US$0.6440/47, compared with a pattern of movement between 0.6420 and 0.6430 before the data's mid-morning release.
Deutsche Morgan Grenfell chief economist Ulf Schoefisch told Reuters Financial Television the kiwi was showing "interesting resilience" around 0.6440.
"I think probably at this point, with the interest rate structure the way it is, we've seen most of the weakness in the currency. I think it will stabilise at these levels," he said after the data.

The RBNZ is widely seen easing monetary policy in the coming months, reflecting the hiatus in the economy and benign inflation pressures, but several commentators had predicted the bank might make an easing statement on Tuesday if the jobs data came in as weak as they expected.
Instead, shortly after the data release, the bank reaffirmed to Reuters that it had not changed its position at all since it delivered its June Monetary Policy Statement.
The next obvious opportunity for it to change its position would be when it releases its September 18 Economic Projections.
Bill Murdoch, head of foreign exchange at ANZ Investment Bank, said money markets would still be looking for another official easing, but "it becomes a timing issue now -- later rather than sooner".
Murdoch said there was room for further falls in the currency if the Economic Projections sanctioned a policy easing as the market hoped.
"I can see that happening, but I don't see another five percent (fall) that we've already had. I think the main correction is essentially over and we might see it more now in a new range."
Murdoch suggested the kiwi was now in a 64-65 U.S. cent range, compared to its recent 68-69 cent range.
"I don't think we are going to down to the 61-63 (area). I think it will be more of a case of 63.5-65."
First NZ Capital managing director of sales and trading Peter Keenan said there was still scope for the currency to fall up to five percent further.

"I guess this data being a bit stronger than expected makes that less of a concern in the short run, but I don't think it greatly changes the view that in fact the economy is very weak at the moment," Keenan said.
